# Release

![Systems Organ Focus: Stage 7 (Defensible Release Gate, ODD Qualification & CAE Safety Case).](figures/fig_pipeline_locator.pdf){#fig-locator-ch11 width=100%}

::: {.callout-objective}
By the conclusion of this chapter, you will be able to:

1. **Formalize Operational Design Domains (ODD):** Specify explicit environmental, kinematic, and sensor boundaries ($\mathcal{X}_{\text{ODD}}$) within which autonomous closed-loop operation is mathematically and physically verified.
2. **Execute the 4-Rung Qualification Ladder:** Progress candidate physical AI policies systematically through Historical Replay $\to$ Domain-Randomized Physics Simulation $\to$ Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) Plant Emulation $\to$ Shadow Fleet Deployment.
3. **Conduct System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA):** Identify causal losses, system hazards, and the four canonical classes of Unsafe Control Actions (UCAs) governing multi-rate embodied architectures.
4. **Execute Cross-Layer Seeded Fault Injection:** Program automated bench campaigns injecting camera dropouts, PTP clock skews, DMA memory bus starvation, Linux kernel panics, and torque disturbances to verify $100\%$ real-time MCU safety containment.
5. **Construct Claim-Argument-Evidence (CAE) Cases & Issue Release Verdicts (`REL-01`):** Synthesize empirical bench logs, latency tail profiles, and fault logs into an accountable **Deploy / Condition / Refuse** release verdict for the final milestone of the Cumulative Design Dossier.
:::

::: {.callout-autopsy}
* **System:** Fleet of 30 Autonomous Urban Delivery Rovers (Vision-Language-Action Policy v1.4)
* **Incident:** Rover accelerated into an oncoming bicycle lane at $4.8\text{ m/s}$, colliding with a cyclist and causing severe orthopedic trauma and a total chassis destruction.
* **Telemetry Snapshot:** The candidate policy achieved a $99.4\%$ task success rate across 10,000 hours of domain-randomized physics simulation. In field deployment on wet asphalt under sudden afternoon rain, road spray coated the stereo depth camera lenses, while tire-to-surface friction plummeted from nominal $\mu = 0.82$ to $\mu = 0.24$.
* **Root Cause:** Mud occlusion induced high-frequency spatial hallucination in the Vision Transformer backbone, while reduced friction expanded physical stopping distance $d_{\text{stop}}$ from $0.45\text{ m}$ to $1.85\text{ m}$. The real-time microcontroller safety enforcer lacked an independent exteroceptive friction estimator and received no hardware camera-health fault signal from the Linux application processor.
* **Architectural Flaw:** The release review board granted unconditional deployment authority based solely on simulation metrics without subjecting the target embedded silicon to cross-layer Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) fault injection or freezing an explicit Operational Design Domain (ODD).
* **Provenance:** Engineered composite. The mechanism and the failure path are drawn from documented incident classes; the system, telemetry, and costs are constructed for teaching and are not a report of a specific event.

**The Sim-to-Real Delta:**
* **What Simulation Assumes:** Physical environments follow deterministic differential equations; sensors deliver perfect pixel grids without optical glare or lens fouling; compute hardware is an idealized infinite-bandwidth Turing machine that never suffers bus contention, memory fragmentation, or operating system kernel panics.
* **What the Bench Measures:** Real cameras suffer frame drops and blinding sunlight; direct memory access (DMA) streams saturate the shared memory bus, inflating inference tails from $P_{50} = 22\text{ ms}$ to $P_{99.9} = 185\text{ ms}$; surface friction changes unpredictably with temperature and moisture; and edge processors undergo thermal throttling that cuts compute clocks by $50\%$ under sustained motor vibration and ambient heat.

## Operational Design Domain (ODD) Specification and Boundary Freezing

An autonomous physical AI agent cannot be certified as "universally safe." A neural network that manipulates warehouse boxes under diffuse indoor LED illumination will hallucinate wildly when struck by direct solar glare; a mobile base calibrated for dry concrete will slide uncontrollably on wet epoxy. Safety in physical systems is strictly contingent upon operating within a mathematically bounded and empirically verified **Operational Design Domain (ODD)** [@leveson2011engineering].

We define the Operational Design Domain $\mathcal{X}_{\text{ODD}}$ as a compact subset of the multi-dimensional environment, kinematic, and electrical state space:

$$\mathcal{X}_{\text{ODD}} = \left\{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^k \;\middle|\; x_{i,\text{min}} \le x_i \le x_{i,\text{max}}, \quad \forall i \in \{1, \dots, k\} \right\} \subset \mathbb{R}^k$$

Operating outside $\mathcal{X}_{\text{ODD}}$ renders all learned spatial representations, forward-invariant control barrier functions, and stopping distance guarantees invalid.

| Environmental & Physical Dimension | Unit | Nominal Operating Envelope ($\mathcal{X}_{\text{ODD}}$) | Out-of-ODD Boundary Trigger | Real-Time Monitor Substrate |
| :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **Ambient Illumination ($E_{\text{lux}}$)** | $\text{Lux}$ | $150 \le E_{\text{lux}} \le 2500$ | $E_{\text{lux}} < 50$ (Darkness) or $E_{\text{lux}} > 10{,}000$ (Blinding Glare) | Hardware Photodiode (MCU ADC, 1000 Hz) |
| **Surface Friction Coefficient ($\mu$)** | — | $0.45 \le \mu \le 0.95$ | $\mu < 0.30$ (Wet epoxy, oil, gravel) | Proprioceptive Wheel Slip Estimator (MCU, 500 Hz) |
| **Workspace Ambient Temp ($T_{\text{amb}}$)** | $^\circ\text{C}$ | $5.0 \le T_{\text{amb}} \le 40.0$ | $T_{\text{amb}} < 0.0$ or $T_{\text{amb}} > 50.0$ (Thermal derating knee) | On-board I2C Thermal Sensor (MCU, 10 Hz) |
| **Motor Winding Temp ($T_{\text{motor}}$)** | $^\circ\text{C}$ | $20.0 \le T_{\text{motor}} \le 85.0$ | $T_{\text{motor}} > 105.0$ (Insulation degradation limit) | Motor Thermistor / ADC (MCU ISR, 1000 Hz) |
| **Battery Bus Voltage ($V_{\text{bus}}$)** | $\text{V}$ | $11.8 \le V_{\text{bus}} \le 14.6$ | $V_{\text{bus}} < 10.5$ (Brownout / Inverter desaturation) | Inverter Voltage Telemetry (MCU SPI, 1000 Hz) |
| **Dynamic Obstacle Velocity ($v_{\text{obs}}$)** | $\text{m/s}$ | $0.0 \le v_{\text{obs}} \le 1.2$ | $v_{\text{obs}} > 2.0$ (High-speed approaching hazard) | Time-of-Flight / Radar Tracker (MCU SPI, 100 Hz) |
| **Maximum Payload Mass ($m_{\text{load}}$)** | $\text{kg}$ | $0.0 \le m_{\text{load}} \le 3.5$ | $m_{\text{load}} > 4.2$ (Structural / Torque limit breach) | Joint Torque Observer (MCU ISR, 1000 Hz) |

: **Operational Design Domain (ODD) specification for the autonomous handling agent.** Parameters are continuously monitored by dedicated hardware channels on the real-time microcontroller. {#tbl-odd-spec}

### Dual-Tier ODD Monitoring and Graceful Degradation

To enforce the ODD boundary without relying on the untrusted Linux application processor, the real-time microcontroller (MCU) executes a zero-allocation **ODD Health Monitor** inside its 1000 Hz timer interrupt service routine (ISR):

1. **Interoceptive Health Monitors:** Direct hardware sampling of internal battery bus voltages, inverter gate-driver temperatures, motor winding temperatures, and memory buffer occupancies. If $T_{\text{motor}} > 85^\circ\text{C}$, the MCU derates maximum allowable continuous torque $\tau_{\text{cont}}$ via active thermal scaling.
2. **Exteroceptive Boundary Monitors:** Low-overhead processing of photodiode illumination, wheel slip velocity differentials ($\Delta v_{\text{wheel}} = |r \omega - v_{\text{chassis}}| > \epsilon_{\text{slip}}$), and direct ultrasonic/radar distance fields.

When any state variable breaches its out-of-ODD trigger boundary ($x_i \notin \mathcal{X}_{\text{ODD}}$), the MCU safety core immediately revokes the MPU's proposal lease and transitions through a deterministic fallback escalation:

$$\text{ODD State Transition} = \begin{cases}
\text{Nominal Autonomous Mode}, & \mathbf{x}(t) \in \mathcal{X}_{\text{ODD}} \\
\text{Category 2 Controlled Speed Derating}, & \mathbf{x}(t) \in \partial \mathcal{X}_{\text{ODD}} \quad (\text{Boundary Proximity}) \\
\text{Category 1 Dynamic Deceleration to Halt}, & \mathbf{x}(t) \notin \mathcal{X}_{\text{ODD}} \quad (\text{Out-of-ODD Fault}) \\
\text{Category 0 Relay Cut \& Mechanical Lock}, & \text{Critical Hardware Electrical / Thermal Breach}
\end{cases}$$

## The 4-Rung Qualification Ladder: From Offline Replay to Shadow Fleets

A foundational error in machine learning is assuming that high benchmark score on a static test split translates to physical safety in closed-loop actuation. In physical AI, software verification requires ascending a rigorous **4-Rung Qualification Ladder**, moving progressively from offline datasets to production hardware in active fleets (@fig-qualification-ladder).

![**The 4-Rung Qualification Ladder for Physical AI Systems.** Progressive promotion gates require passing static offline replay, domain-randomized physics simulation, real-time hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) fault containment, and passive shadow fleet operation before issuing an accountable release verdict.](figures/fig11_qualification_ladder.pdf){#fig-qualification-ladder width=100%}

### Rung 1: Historical Deterministic Log Replay

* **Execution Substrate:** High-performance offline GPU servers evaluating recorded, immutable multimodal sensor streams collected from historical operational runs.
* **Systems Purpose:** Evaluates spatial affordance localization accuracy, latent JEPA world model prediction error, token loss convergence, and offline execution latency.
* **The Fundamental Limitation:** Historical replay is purely open loop. The actions proposed by the candidate model cannot mutate the recorded sensory frames. If the model proposes an erroneous steering trajectory, the logged camera frames continue driving straight. Offline replay is completely blind to closed-loop dynamic divergence, cumulative error drift, and physical inertia ($W_t \to W_{t+1}$).
* **Promotion Gate 0 Requirement:** Spatial 3D affordance error $< 2.0\text{ cm}$; zero unhandled exceptions or NaN tensor outputs over $100{,}000$ historical test frames.

### Rung 2: Physics Simulation with Domain Randomization

* **Execution Substrate:** Highly parallelized rigid-body physics engines (such as MuJoCo or Isaac Sim) executing thousands of concurrent closed-loop rollout episodes on server GPU clusters.
* **Systems Purpose:** Tests closed-loop dynamical stability, obstacle collision avoidance, control barrier function compliance, and multi-modal policy generalization across randomized environmental distributions $\xi \sim \mathcal{D}_{\text{sim}}$.
* **Domain Randomization Formulation:**

$$\xi = \left\{ m_{\text{payload}} \sim \mathcal{U}(0.5, 3.5)\text{ kg}, \; \mu \sim \mathcal{U}(0.35, 0.95), \; \tau_{\text{delay}} \sim \mathcal{U}(15, 65)\text{ ms}, \; \mathbf{w}_{\text{ext}} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_w^2) \right\}$$

* **The Fundamental Limitation:** The Sim-to-Real Reality Gap. Contact dynamics, mechanical backlash, rolling friction hysteresis, non-linear motor saturation, and optical sensor noise are heavily idealized in simulation. Crucially, simulation executes on host CPU/GPU threads with idealized memory architectures, completely masking real-world silicon phenomena such as DMA bus contention, cache misses, SPI bus bit-flips, and Linux operating system jitter.
* **Promotion Gate 1 Requirement:** $\ge 98.0\%$ task completion success rate and zero simulated kinematic collisions across $\ge 10{,}000$ randomized rollout episodes.

### Rung 3: Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) with Plant Emulation

* **Execution Substrate:** The actual target embedded production hardware—the production Linux MPU (e.g., ARM Cortex-A53/A72) and real-time safety MCU (e.g., ARM Cortex-M4/M7)—mounted on a test bench and wired over real physical buses (MIPI CSI-2, SPI, CAN-FD, RPMSG) to a deterministic $10\text{ kHz}$ FPGA/DSP plant emulator.
* **Systems Purpose:** Exposes the physical silicon to genuine computational constraints, interconnect bus arbitration, shared SRAM access latency, realistic DMA bus saturation, and automated cross-layer fault injection.
* **The HIL Plant Loop:** The FPGA real-time plant emulator executes stiff numerical integration of the physical robot's equations of motion at $10\text{ kHz}$:

$$\mathbf{M}(\mathbf{q}) \ddot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{q}, \dot{\mathbf{q}})\dot{\mathbf{q}} + \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{q}) = \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{actuator}} + \boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{disturb}}$$

The emulator synthesizes physical encoder quadrature pulses, motor phase currents, and camera frame DMA packets in hard real time, responding directly to the PWM gate signals driven by the physical MCU.

* **Promotion Gate 2 Requirement:** $100\%$ deterministic containment of all injected hardware, bus, compute, and sensory fault vectors across $\ge 1{,}000$ automated HIL test cycles; zero physical collision envelope breaches ($d_{\text{gap}} > 0$).

### Rung 4: Shadow Fleet Deployment

* **Execution Substrate:** Real physical robots operating inside the genuine target operational environment (e.g., active production warehouse), executing missions under the control of a certified baseline policy or human supervisor.
* **Systems Purpose:** The candidate experimental physical AI model runs entirely in the background (Shadow Mode) on live onboard camera streams and proprioceptive sensors, emitting candidate trajectory buffers $\mathbf{p}_{\text{shadow}}(t)$ without actuator authority.
* **Divergence Metrology:** Telemetry engines continuously compute the instantaneous divergence between the shadow model's proposals and the active baseline controller:

$$\Delta_{\text{divergence}}(t) = \| \mathbf{p}_{\text{shadow}}(t) - \mathbf{u}_{\text{active}}(t) \|_2$$

When $\Delta_{\text{divergence}}(t)$ exceeds an auditing threshold $\epsilon_{\text{audit}}$, the flight data recorder automatically preserves a 5-second synchronized telemetry snippet (sensor frames, latent embeddings, and kinematic traces) for human expert safety review.

* **Promotion Gate 3 Requirement:** Zero uncontained divergent proposals that would violate Control Barrier Function invariants ($h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0$) over $\ge 500$ cumulative operating hours in production shadow fleet operation.

| Qualification Rung | Primary Execution Substrate | Closed-Loop Dynamics? | Target Silicon Timing? | Real Sensory Optics? | Promotion Gate Metric |
| :--- | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- |
| **Rung 1: Log Replay** | Offline GPU Server | No | No | Yes (Recorded) | Gate 0: Affordance error $< 2\text{ cm}$ |
| **Rung 2: Physics Sim** | MuJoCo / Isaac Sim Cluster | Yes | No | No (Synthetic) | Gate 1: $> 98\%$ task success ($10^4$ seeds) |
| **Rung 3: HIL Emulation** | Target MPU + MCU + FPGA | Yes | **Yes** | Emulated | Gate 2: **$100\%$ fault containment** ($10^3$ runs) |
| **Rung 4: Shadow Fleet** | Physical Fleet in Real ODD | Yes | **Yes** | **Yes** | Gate 3: **0 safety breaches over $500\text{ hrs}$** |

: **Summary of the 4-Rung Qualification Ladder.** Progressive promotion ensures that software metrics are systematically validated on embedded silicon before real-world actuation. {#tbl-qualification-ladder}

## System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) for Physical AI

Traditional hazard analysis methodologies like Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA) assume that system failures originate from individual mechanical or electrical component breakdowns (e.g., a broken wire or snapped bolt). In physical AI systems, catastrophic failures frequently occur when **every component operates exactly as designed**, but unsafe interactions emerge between stochastic neural policies, asynchronous multi-rate runtimes, and physical dynamics [@leveson2011engineering].

We apply **System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA)** to systematically uncover unsafe control interactions across the 7 canonical organs of our physical AI architecture.

```
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                          STPA HIERARCHICAL CONTROL STRUCTURE                |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                                                                             |
|   +---------------------------------------------------------------------+   |
|   |                       HUMAN SUPERVISOR                              |   |
|   |  - Commands Mission Intent & Workspace Boundaries                    |   |
|   |  - Retains Unconditional Bumpless Joystick Override & E-Stop        |   |
|   +---------------------------------------------------------------------+   |
|                                     | Control Commands (Heartbeat, Consent) |
|                                     v Feedback (Visual Telemetry, Audible)  |
|   +---------------------------------------------------------------------+   |
|   |             DELIBERATION & PLANNING (Linux MPU / NPU)               |   |
|   |  - Ingests 30 Hz Camera DMA Pixels -> Spatial Tokens                |   |
|   |  - Computes 20 Hz VLA Diffusion Action Chunks (p_t)                 |   |
|   |  - Emits Expiring Intent Leases over Shared IPC Ring Buffer         |   |
|   +---------------------------------------------------------------------+   |
|                                     | Candidate Trajectory Proposals (p_t)  |
|                                     v Enforcer Health / Status Echo         |
|   +---------------------------------------------------------------------+   |
|   |             REAL-TIME SAFETY ENFORCER (Bare-Metal MCU)              |   |
|   |  - 1000 Hz Zero-Allocation Control Barrier Invariant: h(x) >= 0     |   |
|   |  - Dynamic Stopping Distance Verification: d_gap > d_stop           |   |
|   |  - Hardware Watchdog Timer & Category 0/1/2 Stop State Machine      |   |
|   +---------------------------------------------------------------------+   |
|                                     | Permitted Phase Voltages / Gate PWM   |
|                                     v Inverter Current / Encoder Feedback   |
|   +---------------------------------------------------------------------+   |
|   |                     PHYSICAL ACTUATORS & PLANT                      |   |
|   |  - Permanent Magnet Synchronous Motors + Inverters                  |   |
|   |  - Spring-Loaded Electromagnetic Friction Brakes                    |   |
|   |  - State Mutation: W_t -> W_{t+1} (Kinetic Momentum & Friction)     |   |
|   +---------------------------------------------------------------------+   |
|                                                                             |
+-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

### System Losses and Hazards

We define the primary catastrophic losses ($L$) and system-level hazards ($H$):

* **Loss $L_1$:** Human fatality, physical injury, or occupational harm.
* **Loss $L_2$:** Structural destruction of robot chassis, tooling, or facility equipment.
* **Loss $L_3$:** Loss of mission operational integrity or catastrophic payload destruction.
* **Hazard $H_1$:** Robot kinetic energy exceeds safe threshold ($E_k > 50\text{ J}$) during human co-occupancy within workspace clearance envelope ($d_{\text{clearance}} < 0.50\text{ m}$).
* **Hazard $H_2$:** Actuator torque commands exceed structural limits, inducing joint over-travel or mechanical gearbox gear-tooth shear.
* **Hazard $H_3$:** Mobile base velocity violates surface traction envelope ($v > \sqrt{\mu g R_{\text{turn}}}$), inducing uncontrolled skid or vehicle rollover.

### The 4 Canonical Unsafe Control Actions (UCAs)

STPA evaluates every control action issued across architectural interfaces against four canonical failure modes:

| Control Action | UCA-1: Not Providing Action | UCA-2: Providing Too Early / Too Late / Out of Sequence | UCA-3: Providing Wrong Control Action | UCA-4: Stopping Action Too Soon / Applying Too Long |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **MPU Action Chunk Proposal ($\mathbf{p}_t$)** | MPU hangs during obstacle avoidance maneuver, providing zero updated trajectory ($H_1$). | MPU emits trajectory chunk after stale observation deadline ($\Delta t > t_{\text{expire}}$), causing delayed reaction ($H_1$). | VLA policy hallucinates inverted coordinate frame, proposing positive acceleration toward obstacle ($H_1, H_2$). | MPU holds high-speed driving command after target waypoint has been reached ($H_2$). |
| **MCU CBF Barrier Filter ($u_t = \text{QP}(\mathbf{p}_t)$)** | MCU fails to project violating candidate action onto safe set $\mathcal{C}$, permitting illegal torque command ($H_1, H_2$). | MCU applies barrier intervention after stopping distance has already exceeded available gap ($d_{\text{stop}} > d_{\text{gap}}$) ($H_1$). | MCU QP solver computes infeasible relaxation, outputting unbounded torque step that trips motor overcurrent ($H_2$). | MCU releases dynamic braking torque before the physical mechanism reaches zero velocity ($v > 0$) ($H_1, H_3$). |
| **Human Joystick Takeover** | Supervisor fails to press E-stop during visible out-of-ODD excursion ($H_1$). | Human operator takes over without bumpless blending filter, inducing severe mechanical torque spike ($H_2$). | Operator deflects joystick in wrong direction during emergency maneuver ($H_1$). | Human releases dead-man consent switch before autonomous policy has safely re-armed ($H_1$). |
| **Hardware E-Stop Relay** | Relay contacts weld shut, failing to disconnect motor DC bus power upon watchdog timeout ($H_1, L_1$). | Relay opens prematurely during high-speed turn, causing uncontrolled dynamic spin ($H_3$). | MCU commands software reset instead of opening physical power relays ($H_1$). | Mechanical friction brakes disengage before motor back-EMF has fully dissipated ($H_2$). |

: **STPA Unsafe Control Action (UCA) matrix across the physical AI architecture.** Each UCA traces directly to a system-level hazard ($H_1, H_2, H_3$) and requires an independent hardware or algorithmic constraint. {#tbl-stpa-uca}

## Cross-Layer Seeded Fault Injection Campaigns

Software unit testing verifies that functions return expected outputs under nominal arguments. It proves absolutely nothing about how an embedded physical system behaves when a memory bus saturates, a camera cable vibrates loose, or an operating system kernel panics while the robot is carrying a $3.5\text{ kg}$ payload at $1.5\text{ m/s}$.

To establish defensible release assurance, the candidate system must be subjected to an automated **Cross-Layer Seeded Fault Injection Campaign** on the Hardware-in-the-Loop test bench (@fig-cross-layer-faults).

![**Cross-Layer Seeded Fault Injection Architecture.** Faults are systematically injected across four distinct layers (Sensory, Compute/Bus, Model/VLA, and Electrical/Physical) into the target dual-brain platform (Linux MPU + Real-Time MCU). The real-time MCU safety reflex must deterministically contain $100\%$ of injected fault vectors without violating physical safety envelopes.](figures/fig11_cross_layer_faults.pdf){#fig-cross-layer-faults width=100%}

### The 4 Fault Injection Layers

Fault injection must traverse the entire vertical systems stack, targeting every physical and logical boundary:

#### Layer 1: Sensory and Transduction Faults
* **Injected Perturbations:** Intentional dropping of MIPI CSI-2 camera frames for durations $\Delta t \in [50, 500]\text{ ms}$; synthetic optical blooming/saturation ($E_{\text{lux}} \to 15{,}000\text{ Lux}$); IEEE-1588 PTP hardware clock skew ($\Delta t_{\text{skew}} > 5\text{ ms}$); simulated mud spatters obscuring $> 40\%$ of depth pixels.
* **Containment Expectation:** The sensory pipeline detects missing frame timestamps via seqlock timeouts; the MPU invalidates its spatial affordance tokens and notifies the MCU; the MCU transitions to proprioceptive position hold within $20\text{ ms}$.

#### Layer 2: Compute, Bus and Operating System Faults
* **Injected Perturbations:** Forcible injection of Linux kernel panics (`kill -9` on vision daemon, kernel null-pointer dereference); synthetic DMA memory bus saturation flooding LPDDR5 channels at $4.5\text{ GB/s}$; non-deterministic dynamic allocation (`malloc`) latency stalls; intentional SPI/CAN-FD CRC checksum bit-flips.
* **Containment Expectation:** The Linux MPU hangs or misses its heartbeat update. The dedicated hardware watchdog timer on the MCU expires ($t_{\text{watchdog}} > 50\text{ ms}$); the MCU executes a non-maskable interrupt (NMI), bypasses all software stacks, and triggers a Category 1 controlled dynamic stop.

#### Layer 3: Model and Algorithmic Faults
* **Injected Perturbations:** Synthetic injection of out-of-distribution visual adversarial noise causing the Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy to hallucinate 3D target coordinates outside the workspace ($\|\mathbf{p}_{\text{target}}\| > 2.0\text{ m}$); insertion of discontinuous velocity steps ($\Delta \dot{\mathbf{q}} > 10\text{ rad/s}$); corrupted diffusion action chunks.
* **Containment Expectation:** The candidate proposal passes to the MCU safety enforcer. The 1000 Hz Control Barrier Function (CBF) quadratic program clips the proposed action to the workspace bounding hull, while the jerk-limited rate limiter clamps the command to $j_{\text{max}} = 20\text{ rad/s}^3$.

#### Layer 4: Electrical and Physical Faults
* **Injected Perturbations:** Simulated motor driver over-temperature flag ($T_{\text{inverter}} > 105^\circ\text{C}$); battery DC bus voltage sag ($V_{\text{bus}} \to 9.8\text{ V}$); sudden external collision load torque spike ($\tau_{\text{ext}} > 35\text{ Nm}$); incremental optical encoder phase line disconnect.
* **Containment Expectation:** Interoceptive ADC monitors on the MCU trip instantaneous hardware current derating; motor gate driver PWM outputs are pulled low within $150\,\mu\text{s}$; mechanical spring brakes engage.

### Mathematical Containment Formulation and Pass Criteria

Let $\mathcal{F}_{\text{injected}} = \{ f_1, f_2, \dots, f_N \}$ denote the set of all cross-layer injected fault scenarios. Let $\mathbf{x}(t)$ denote the physical state trajectory of the robot under fault $f_k$, and let $h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0$ define the forward-invariant safety barrier certificate.

The system satisfies the **Deterministic Fault Containment Contract** if and only if:

$$\forall f_k \in \mathcal{F}_{\text{injected}}, \quad \begin{cases}
h(\mathbf{x}(t)) \ge 0, & \forall t \ge 0 \\
d_{\text{gap}}(t) > 0, & \forall t \ge 0 \quad (\text{Zero Physical Collision}) \\
t_{\text{stop}} \le t_{\text{delay}} + \frac{v(t_{\text{fault}})}{a_{\text{max}}}, & (\text{Bounded Stopping Time})
\end{cases}$$

$$\text{Containment Rate } R_{\text{contain}} = \frac{N_{\text{safe}}}{N_{\text{total}}} = 1.0000 \quad (100.0\%)$$

Any single uncontained fault scenario where $h(\mathbf{x}) < 0$, a physical collision occurs ($d_{\text{gap}} \le 0$), or the mechanism fails to come to a controlled halt represents an immediate, non-negotiable **Gate Failure** that triggers a **REFUSE** release verdict.

## Constructing the Claim-Argument-Evidence (CAE) Safety Case

A pile of test logs is not a safety argument. Regulators, system safety certifiers, and cross-disciplinary review boards cannot evaluate unstructured telemetry files. Defensible engineering requires structuring assurance through a formal **Claim-Argument-Evidence (CAE)** framework [@bishop1998methodology], establishing an unbroken chain of reasoning from top-level claims down to measured bench data (@fig-cae-safety-case).

![**The Claim-Argument-Evidence (CAE) Safety Case Architecture.** The top-level claim ($C_{\text{top}}$) decomposes into four rigorous argument pillars ($A_1$ through $A_4$), each backed by immutable bench metrology artifacts ($E_1$ through $E_4$). The complete structure terminates in an accountable release decision signed by the cross-disciplinary review board.](figures/fig11_cae_safety_case.pdf){#fig-cae-safety-case width=100%}

### The 4 Pillars of the Physical AI Safety Case

The safety case decomposes the top-level deployment claim into four load-bearing engineering arguments:

#### Top-Level Safety Claim ($C_{\text{top}}$)
> *"The Physical AI Agent (Model v1.0 / Firmware Bank A) is acceptably safe for autonomous manipulation and transport operations within the frozen Operational Design Domain $\mathcal{X}_{\text{ODD-01}}$."*

#### Argument Pillar 1: Deterministic Fault Containment ($A_1$)
* **Argument Formulation:** All single-point hardware, software, and communication failures on the untrusted Linux MPU or interconnect buses are deterministically arrested by the independent real-time MCU safety core within $t_{\text{contain}} \le 50\text{ ms}$ without kinematic collision.
* **Supporting Evidence ($E_1$):** Complete automated HIL fault injection campaign logs: $1000/1000$ seeded faults safely contained ($R_{\text{contain}} = 1.000$); maximum observed stopping time under kernel panic $t_{\text{stop}} = 42\text{ ms}$; zero barrier violations ($h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0$).

#### Argument Pillar 2: Freshness and Tail Latency Bounds ($A_2$)
* **Argument Formulation:** The end-to-end sense-to-actuation latency distribution satisfies hard real-time deadlines such that $P_{99.9}$ latency $\Delta t_{\text{wall}} \le 80\text{ ms}$, ensuring physical dynamic stopping distance $d_{\text{stop}}(v, \Delta t)$ never breaches environmental clearance margins.
* **Supporting Evidence ($E_2$):** Empirical bench metrology latency CDF (from `REQ-01`): $P_{50} = 22.4\text{ ms}$, $P_{90} = 34.1\text{ ms}$, $P_{99.9} = 72.0\text{ ms} < 80.0\text{ ms}$; minimum verified physical stopping clearance margin $\Delta d_{\text{margin}} = +18.5\text{ cm}$.

#### Argument Pillar 3: Unconditional Human Governance ($A_3$)
* **Argument Formulation:** Human operators retain instantaneous, un-preemptible authority to override autonomous execution at any millisecond via hardware E-stop circuits and bumpless joystick intervention filters.
* **Supporting Evidence ($E_3$):** Telemetry records (from `AUTH-01`): $50/50$ seamless joystick overrides executed under full actuator load; peak override jerk $\| \dddot{\mathbf{q}} \| = 12.4\text{ rad/s}^3 < 20.0\text{ rad/s}^3$; tamper-evident SHA-256 telemetry lineage log binding model weights to training runs.

#### Argument Pillar 4: Real-Time ODD Boundary Enforcement ($A_4$)
* **Argument Formulation:** Dedicated hardware interoceptive and exteroceptive monitors detect environmental or thermal excursions outside $\mathcal{X}_{\text{ODD}}$ and transition the machine into safe speed-derating or controlled stopping before hazardous dynamic regimes are reached.
* **Supporting Evidence ($E_4$):** Bench ODD excursion logs: Optical blinding glare detected in $< 18\text{ ms}$; surface slip trigger engaged Category 1 braking in $< 25\text{ ms}$; thermal derating verified at $T_{\text{motor}} = 85^\circ\text{C}$.

## The Accountable Release Review Board and Release Verdicts

The culmination of the entire systems engineering process is the formal **Release Gate Review**. The review board brings together four distinct engineering perspectives, eliminating organizational blind spots:

1. **Embedded Silicon & Real-Time Systems Lead:** Verifies zero dynamic memory allocation (`malloc`), bounded ISR execution cycles ($< 250\,\mu\text{s}$), hardware watchdog timer non-maskable interrupts, and memory bus QoS arbitration.
2. **Embodied AI & Machine Learning Lead:** Verifies model affordance accuracy, dataset training lineage, domain-randomized simulation convergence, and shadow mode divergence statistics.
3. **System Safety & Regulatory Lead:** Verifies STPA hazard mitigation traceability, Control Barrier Function mathematical proofs, HIL fault containment logs, and ODD boundary enforcement.
4. **Human Factors & Operational UX Lead:** Verifies bumpless joystick transfer dynamics, dead-man consent switch timing, emergency stop ergonomics, and intervention logging schemas.

### The 3 Release Verdicts

The review board evaluates the complete cumulative design dossier (`LOOP-01` through `REL-01`) and issues one of three formal, legally accountable verdicts:

* **1. DEPLOY (Unconditional Production Release):**
  * *Condition:* All four promotion gates passed; $100\%$ HIL fault containment achieved; $P_{99.9}$ latency tail strictly within budget; all four board leads vote "PASS".
  * *Operational Authority:* The system is authorized for fully autonomous closed-loop physical operations within the frozen Operational Design Domain $\mathcal{X}_{\text{ODD}}$.
* **2. CONDITION (Restricted / Conditional Release):**
  * *Condition:* Core safety invariants ($h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0$) and fault containment are verified, but edge-case ODD parameters (e.g., low-light performance or high-speed braking margins) require operational restrictions.
  * *Operational Authority:* Release permitted under legally binding operational constraints: maximum speed derated to $v_{\text{max}} \le 0.25\text{ m/s}$; operation prohibited in ambient illumination $< 300\text{ Lux}$; designated safety supervisor required within visual line of sight with wireless E-stop.
* **3. REFUSE (Deployment Blocked):**
  * *Condition:* Any single uncontained fault in HIL testing; $P_{99.9}$ latency tail violates stopping distance envelope ($d_{\text{stop}} > d_{\text{gap}}$); missing data lineage hashes; or any board lead votes "REJECT".
  * *Operational Authority:* Firmware flashing to production flash Bank A is cryptographically blocked. The system is returned to engineering with a mandatory architectural remedy notice.

## Systems Fallacies and Pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning}
### Common Engineering Fallacies
* **Fallacy 1: "High benchmark accuracy on a static test dataset proves a model is safe to deploy."**  
  *Correction:* Static datasets measure open-loop pattern recognition on fixed pixels. They evaluate zero closed-loop dynamics, cannot measure physical momentum, and are completely blind to DMA bus contention, sensor dropouts, and hardware latency tails.
* **Fallacy 2: "If a robot succeeds across 10,000 simulation episodes, it will succeed on real hardware."**  
  *Correction:* Physics simulators idealize contact dynamics, motor back-EMF, and compute timing. Simulation cannot reproduce real-world lens mud, thermal clock throttling, or operating system thread preemption. Simulation is Rung 2—only Rung 3 (HIL) and Rung 4 (Shadow Mode) provide physical evidence.
* **Fallacy 3: "Safety can be added at the end of the project by wrapping the AI model in a Python guard script."**  
  *Correction:* A software safety guard running in Python on a non-real-time Linux operating system is subject to the same kernel crashes, scheduling stalls, and memory corruption as the model itself. Safety must be architecturally isolated on dedicated bare-metal microcontroller hardware executing deterministic, zero-allocation barrier invariants.
:::

### Hands-on Realization: Lab 11 — The Cross-Layer Fault Injection Rig
Deploy the complete physical AI software stack onto the **Arduino UNO Q Dual-Brain Kit** (Linux MPU + ARM Cortex-M4 MCU). Using the companion laboratory rig ([`labs/11-fault-injection-rig`](../../../labs/11-authority-paths/CONTRACT.md)), execute an automated cross-layer fault injection campaign:

1. **Sensory Dropout:** Programmatically drop camera MIPI CSI-2 buffers for $200\text{ ms}$ while commanding high-speed trajectory tracking. Observe how the MCU transitions to proprioceptive position hold.
2. **Compute Crash:** Trigger an intentional Linux kernel panic (`echo c > /proc/sysrq-trigger`) during closed-loop motion. Measure the exact latency from MPU freeze to hardware watchdog trip and motor current cutoff using a digital logic analyzer.
3. **Algorithmic Hallucination:** Inject out-of-workspace trajectory steps ($+300\%$ coordinate step) into the shared IPC ring buffer. Verify that the 1000 Hz MCU Control Barrier Function projects candidate commands onto the safe workspace boundary without mechanical gearbox impact.
4. **Dossier Defense:** Extract the microsecond PTP telemetry logs, construct the complete **Integrated Deployment Case** (`REL-01`), and defend your release verdict before the peer review jury.
:::
